cues.text: In 1342, a violent thunderstorm broke suddenly over the village of Stiphout , in the Dutch province of North Brabant.
A lightning bolt struck St. Trudo’s parish church, setting it ablaze; the elderly pastor, Jan Hocaerts, ran at once to warn neighboring households as flames spread quickly through the building.
A group of parishioners, led by a man named Jan Baloys, resolved to try to save the Blessed Sacrament from the burning church.
With the doors already impassable, the only way in was for someone to be lowered through a window into the fire itself.
The rescuer found the ciborium containing the consecrated Hosts entirely unharmed, even as the fire consumed the altar area around it.
The rescuer carried it safely out to the crowd gathered outside, who are said to have cried out together, "Miracle!"
, upon seeing what had been saved.
A Church Rebuilt, A Relic Later Lost
The parish church was rebuilt following the fire, and the rescued Hosts remained venerated there for over two centuries.

The religious wars and upheavals of the sixteenth century scattered every trace of them by 1557—a loss the community has continued to mark with devotion rather than let the memory fade with the relic itself.
The church, rebuilt again over the centuries, was elevated to a minor basilica by Pope Pius XI in 1938 and remains a pilgrimage site in the Netherlands today.
A painting inside still depicts the original rescue, while the relic's memory is carried forward each year in a procession held on the octave of Corpus Christi.
Though the Hosts themselves are gone, this procession expresses a community's devotion to a sign it can no longer physically show, but has never stopped keeping.
